title: Judges 15:1–8
context: Samson returns to Timnah to claim the Philistine wife he left in anger at the end of chapter 14, only to find she has been given to another man. What follows is a spiral of personal revenge: Samson burns Philistine crops, the Philistines burn his wife and her father, and Samson strikes back with great slaughter. The narrator reports these events frankly. Earlier the text noted that the LORD was seeking "an occasion against the Philistines" (14:4), yet Samson himself acts out of wounded pride.

verses.text: But after a while, in the time of wheat harvest, Samson visited his wife with a young goat. He said, “I will go in to my wife’s room.” But her father wouldn’t allow him to go in.
verses.arminianNotes: Samson arrives at harvest with a young goat, expecting to resume the marriage he abandoned in anger (14:19). Arminian readers note his self-centered impulsiveness. The judge's personal choices are real and morally weighty, not scripted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator has already said the LORD "sought an occasion against the Philistines" (14:4). Samson's careless domestic life becomes, under God's hidden providence, the occasion for Israel's deliverance to begin.

verses.text: Her father said, “I most certainly thought that you utterly hated her; therefore I gave her to your companion. Isn’t her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please, take her instead.”
verses.arminianNotes: The father-in-law's excuse and offer of the younger sister treat the women as bargaining pieces. Arminian readers see the moral confusion of the age, in which both Israelites and Philistines act on self-interest rather than covenant faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the brokenness of the setting. Scripture records this exchange without approving it, showing how deep the disorder runs in a world where people act without regard for God's ways.

verses.text: Samson said to them, “This time I will be blameless in the case of the Philistines when I harm them.”
verses.arminianNotes: "This time I will be blameless" shows Samson justifying revenge as fair retaliation. Arminian readers note that his motive is personal grievance, not zeal for God, a warning about self-justification dressed as righteousness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see personal vengeance here, not a pure calling. They observe that God's purpose to "begin to save Israel" (13:5) moves forward even through Samson's mixed motives, without excusing them.

verses.text: Samson went and caught three hundred foxes, and took torches, and turned tail to tail, and put a torch in the middle between every two tails.
verses.arminianNotes: The foxes and torches are a striking, almost theatrical act of vandalism. Arminian readers see Samson's great gifts used for private retaliation, and note that God-given strength can be misdirected by human choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samson's strength and cunning come from God's appointment, yet he uses them rashly. Scripture shows God giving gifts that their bearer does not always steward well, while God's aims still advance.

verses.text: When he had set the torches on fire, he let them go into the standing grain of the Philistines, and burned up both the shocks and the standing grain, and also the olive groves.
verses.arminianNotes: Burning standing grain, sheaves, and olive groves struck the Philistine economy hard. Arminian readers note that the conflict now harms whole communities, a sign of how personal revenge escalates far beyond its original wrong.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the burned fields as the start of open conflict between Israel's judge and its oppressors. What began as a private quarrel becomes the setting for God to weaken Philistine power over his people.

verses.text: Then the Philistines said, “Who has done this?” They said, “Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he has taken his wife and given her to his companion.” The Philistines came up, and burned her and her father with fire.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines burn the woman and her father, the very fate she feared in 14:15. Arminian readers see how sin breeds violence, with innocent and guilty alike caught in a cycle that neither side will break.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the grim irony: she betrayed Samson to avoid being burned, and it happened anyway. Scripture exposes the folly of trying to secure oneself by deceit apart from God, and the cruelty of the oppressors.

verses.text: Samson said to them, “If you behave like this, surely I will take revenge on you, and after that I will cease.”
verses.arminianNotes: "I will take revenge on you, and after that I will cease" shows Samson believing he can control the cycle. Arminian readers note that revenge rarely ends where we intend; the law reserved vengeance to God (Deuteronomy 32:35).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also point to Deuteronomy 32:35, "Vengeance is mine." Samson's personal vow contrasts with God's just judgment; God will use Samson against the Philistines, but Samson's spirit of revenge is not commended.

verses.text: He struck them hip and thigh with a great slaughter; and he went down and lived in the cave in Etam’s rock.
verses.arminianNotes: "Hip and thigh" is an idiom for a crushing defeat. Samson then withdraws to the cave in Etam's rock. Arminian readers see a judge acting alone, with no call to Israel and no prayer, a picture of gifts without dependence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samson's lone campaigns fit the angel's word that he would only "begin" to save Israel (13:5). God's deliverance through him is real but partial, pointing beyond him to fuller salvation.
